Reviewer #1:

This is a very interesting and timely paper, discussing the important issue of the 'award gap' which is clearly an issue impacting on degree outcomes as well as career progression and opportunity. The paper provides welcome subject-level consideration and generalised policy recommendations to address the issues discussed. I absolutely think it should be published subject to the author addressing a small number of suggested corrections/amendments.Reviewer #2:

This manuscript will be of interest to all academics and leaders of Higher Education Institutes (HEIs) who are engaged in identifying and implementing a ranges of strategies for closing the awarding gap. The data presented in the manuscript clearly provides a basis for the full range of degrees who assess via both examination and coursework to consider the marking differentials between the two methods and their impact on either maintaining, worsening or closing the awarding gap.

The manuscript has the potential of significant impact across a range of degrees, beyond the sciences, due to its exploration of marks at component level and through the comparison of exams and coursework. It does provide a methodology which can be readily replicated across other disciplines and institutions.

A challenge to be considered is the emphasis within the recommendations (policies) around research funding and increased staffing. A great deal of insight has already been achieved with one of the key areas of focus landing on the levels of cultural competence and feelings of identity and belonging which need to be developed and improved within HEI's which although recognised within the recommendations does feature as less significant.

This manuscripts provides a clear overview of the 'race awarding' gap issue within western institutions and provides a clear outline of the range of research undertaken over a 10 year period with little progression in closing the race awarding gap.

The manuscript aims to identify alternative strategies in reducing the gap and certainly the methodology used, as outlined, does provide a different perspective in looking at assessment components. The methodology is clear and can be replicated but only where a combination of course work and examinations make up the assessment components. If a degree, module or specific subject within a degree only utilises one assessment type then the methodology will either not be relevant or will need adaptation.

The manuscript also aims to identify how the alternative strategy will look to reduce gaps in career progression. The outcomes of the study do demonstrate the differences in awarding based on component assessments but what the strategy does not do is be more specific with regards to challenges for career progression for BAME graduates. The narratives around the impact of the awarding gap and the recommendations and policies do provide a direct link to how changing assessment methodologies could improve outcomes and in time career progression but this could be considered as a 'by product' of the alternative strategy.

The HEI sector is currently becoming more aware of issues of racial inequality and the impetus generated by the Black Lives Matter movement both here and across the world has provided a spotlight on these racial inequalities in all sectors and particularly in higher education where the discrimination exacerbates overall life chances of a significant part of the university population. And so although the awarding/attainment gap has been researched, reviewed and action planned for many many years the BLM spotlight has provided a new energy and drive to address this significant inequality with a new and particular focus over the last few years away from the 'student deficit' model and more towards the 'institutional responsibility' model. So in this very current context this work will be particularly relevant in the wider 'race equality' context the sector finds itself in.

The manuscript would be strengthened to deliver on its aim if the connection to awarding gaps for BAME students and their 'academic' career progression were emphasised more in the literature review.Reviewer #3:

This paper provides a detailed breakdown of the awarding gap between BAME students and white students on a cell biology degree programme (with multiple pathways) at a single institution with a large BAME population. This detailed analysis shows that the biggest awarding gap lies in the exam component of the assessment and suggests some policies to close the gap going forward. There are some limitations to the analysis (should include first class marks as well as good honours) and suggested policies (e.g. vagueness around asking for funding) that I will address in detail in my review.In this study, the author examines the awarding gap that exists between BAME students and white students on cell biology degree programs. Unlike previous studies, the research does not just look at overall degree classification but examines individual assessments that make up the degree. The research concludes that it is specifically the exam component of assessment that contributes towards the awarding gap in Cell Biology degrees at UCL. Although these conclusions may not be representative of all programmes and institutions, the study provides a welcome framework to enable others to carry out this kind of detailed analysis if they have not started doing so already and shows that it is possible to carry out these analyses even in complex degree streams and pathways. From the data analysis, clear policy recommendations are put forward although I would caution against advocating more funding into research around 'why' the gap exists and instead repurpose such money for investing in proper resource to tackle the problem including by creating compassionate communities within institutions of BAME students working together with allies who have the power to instigate change.

Specific points – strengths, and issues to address, around data analysis.

1) The introduction sets the context for the pervasive awarding gap (and other factors that may contribute to it) extremely well and raises the issue of variability between subjects.

2) The data is collected from seven student cohorts across all three years of the degrees, including only students who completed the course. All marking for this dataset was carried out by machine or candidate identity-blind, which is a strength of the institution's assessment process as it eliminates human bias, conscious or unconscious.

3) One limitation of the study is perhaps that the cohorts, degree streams, and course selection is very complex as many different types of students take cell biology courses. Given that, the data is analysed appropriately using two different approaches, but that does mean that any nuances around achievement for students on different degree programs (who may experience differently supportive learning environments) is masked.

4) Another limitation is that the data analysis focuses on 'good honours', a first or 2.1 degree. We have carried out similar (unpublished) analyses at my institution that suggest that the 'first class' awarding gap is much bigger than that for good honours. Would it be possible to analyse firsts-only? The current analysis suggests that marking coursework identity-blind (largely) eliminates the awarding gap but (again based on my own data analyses) I wonder if looking at firsts-only would tell a different story. I think that this would be an important addition to the study.

5) I wonder if it is also possible (as this is a large dataset) to disaggregate the ethnicity data. "BAME" is a blanket term that includes groups in addition to people of colour. Moreover, previous data shows that Black students tend to fare worse than, for example, Asian students. Could we specifically look at the awarding gap for Black students is the largest?

6) A thought about the statistical analysis: a t-test is not appropriate for non-parametric (%) data unless normality has been tested for or a correction has been applied. Has this been done? It is not clear from the methods.

7) Showing figure 2c as continuous data points joined by a line is unclear: it would be more consistent to use bars as in Figure

Some thoughts about the discussion and policy recommendations.

I absolutely agree with the suggestions of policy 1 and policy 2. However, Policy 3 needs to be careful and specific otherwise it is not convincing to "Increase Direct Funding to Research the Factors that Cause the Award Gap", in fact I would be tempted to remove this section and expand Policy 2 as outlined in the next couple of paragraphs.

Much "why" research has already been carried out over the last 30 years that all points in the same direction: there are huge systemic, structural barriers that are put in place by people of privilege and power that disadvantage BAME students in education and the problems start before University, although are reinforced in higher education. It is the 'business as usual' approach has to change as this is what causes the problem (see, for example, much of David Gillborn's research including Gillborn et al. (2017)). Racism is subtle, common and can be well intentioned/paternalistic ('we know best how to fix you'). Funding and resource would be better spent on Policy 2 and in addition an interrogation of every process of the academy: the curriculum, appointment processes, assessments, the training delivered around racism – this would probably fit under Policy 2a.

More thoughts on Policy 2a: We need to resource local support that involves the relevant students. Building supportive communities is key. We need to really listen to student experiences of all the academy's processes and involve students in the process of change as collaborators so that barriers can be removed compassionately (Atkinson 2002). My own anecdotal listening plus institutional training shows that BAME students are subject to daily micro-aggressions and more training is needed to increase the number of allies who are confident to call out toxic behaviour. BAME students acutely feel a lack of similar role models in the academy and lack a sense of belonging. Thus, changing recruitment processes is a key step (see policy 5 below).

For policy 4 to work, we need to find people who believe they will benefit from the change and put them in positions of power. Race is an uncomfortable subject for many who are unwilling (consciously or unconsciously) to confront their privilege. It might be worth adding a comment to that effect.

Policy 5: I absolutely agree. I would advocate for policy 5b to include removing the requirement for a 1st class degree to get a PhD place (this is partly why I made my earlier point about extending the data analysis beyond good honours if at all possible) and to do shortlisting for recruitment based on anonymous CVs. More resource needs to go into the training and diversity of recruitment panels. Encouraging more BAME applicants will require more visible role models at higher levels but there is a worry around over burdening the minority with this work perhaps this could be discussed a little too.

results.result: Award gaps between white and BAME students in undergraduate degree outcomes are well-documented internationally. In the UK, the gap is 13.4% (81.4% white vs 68.0% BAME receiving good degrees), has been known for over 25 years, exists at every UK university, and varies by subject (3-22%). Similar gaps are reported in the Netherlands, US, and Australia.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5 and C21 are well-supported by citations to government reports and published studies documenting award gaps across multiple countries and institutions. The quantitative data in C1 provides specific percentages, while C2-C5 and C21 cite multiple independent sources confirming the widespread and persistent nature of these gaps.

results.result: Prior entrance qualifications do not explain the award gap. The gap persists when comparing students with identical entrance qualifications in both UK and US, and even exists for Chinese and Indian students who outperform white students on entrance exams. Analysis of UCL cell biology students with virtually identical A-level scores (BAME: 50.53±0.15, white: 50.29±0.33) confirms this pattern.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C8, C34-C35 are supported by both citations to prior studies and original data from the current study (C29-C33). The convergence of evidence from multiple institutions and the detailed quantitative analysis of A-level entrance scores versus subsequent performance provides strong support that entrance qualifications do not explain the gap.

results.result: Racism or unconscious bias in marking is unlikely to be a major cause of the award gap since most marking is blind. Studies controlling for over 20 factors (poverty, age, school type, learning style) still find a large unexplained gap.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C10 are supported by citations to multiple studies. C9 is strengthened by the fact that marking is typically blind and by studies specifically examining bias. C10 demonstrates that extensive efforts to identify confounding factors have failed to explain the gap, though the claim relies on prior work rather than original analysis.

results.result: The award gap has significant career consequences. White graduates have 33% higher employment rates one year post-graduation. Only 9.1% of professors are BAME (vs 14% population). The largest attrition occurs at undergraduate-to-PhD and PhD-to-postdoc transitions, with fewer BAME students possessing the top grades required for competitive PhD positions.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C16, C19-C20 are supported by citations to government reports and published studies documenting career progression disparities. The claims establish a clear pipeline problem where the undergraduate award gap compounds at critical career transitions, though some claims (C16, C20) involve inference about mechanisms.

results.result: The UCL cell biology cohort studied included 792 students (47.0% BAME, 63.3% UK-domiciled). UCL's award gap for UK students (4.9%) is smaller than the national average (13.4%), and similar to the gap for international students (6.3%), suggesting minimal domicile effect.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C28 present descriptive statistics about the study cohort and institutional context. The data are clearly reported with specific sample sizes and percentages. The comparison between UK and international student gaps (C27-C28) is appropriately cautious in its interpretation.

results.result: BAME and white cell biology students had virtually identical entrance qualifications (mean A-level tariff: BAME 50.53±0.15, white 50.29±0.33; 95.45% vs 95.02% A*/A grades), yet BAME students received lower year 2 cell biology grades (mean low 2i vs high 2i for white students).
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C33 present original quantitative data with appropriate statistical measures (means, SEMs, sample sizes). The data clearly demonstrate equivalent entrance qualifications but divergent outcomes, directly supporting the study's central finding. Figure 1 provides visual confirmation of the reported statistics.

results.result: Across all years (1-3) of cell biology courses studied, proportionally fewer BAME students received good grades than white students. The gap appears by year 1 and the average gaps in cell biology (8-13%) are similar to UCL-wide gaps (7-11%), indicating the findings are representative.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C39 present consistent quantitative findings across multiple cohorts and years, with supporting data from both the specific study and broader institutional context. C37 is strengthened by citation to similar findings at another university. The comparison to UCL-wide data (C38-C39) appropriately contextualizes the findings.

results.result: The award gap is primarily derived from exam performance rather than coursework. In 11/12 sets of marks, exam gaps were larger (year 1: 13%, year 2: 13%, year 3: 17% average). Coursework gaps were 3.1-13.1 times smaller than exam gaps. This pattern was reproducible across cohorts.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C46 present the study's central finding with detailed quantitative evidence across multiple cohorts and years. The consistency of the pattern (11/12 cases) and the magnitude of differences (3-13 fold) provide strong support. The exception (C42-C43) is appropriately explained. Cohen's D analysis (C51) provides additional statistical support for effect size differences.

results.result: The small coursework award gap (1-2%) in years 1-2 likely reflects fluctuations between admission years, while year 3 shows a consistently small gap (5%). Exam gaps persist even when exam and coursework grades are similarly high, and when coursework is expected to be harder, indicating the gap is not simply due to task difficulty.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C50 provide nuanced interpretation of the coursework findings. C47 is explicitly speculative but supported by observed patterns. C48-C50 use the data to rule out alternative explanations (overall performance level, task difficulty), strengthening the conclusion that assessment type matters. The reasoning is logical though some claims involve inference.

results.result: Cohen's D analysis confirmed coursework effects are 3-6 times smaller than exam effects. Detailed analysis at 5% mark intervals revealed no hidden coursework gaps. Exam mark distributions for BAME students were shifted half to one full grade band lower than white students, while coursework distributions were almost completely superimposed.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C56 provide rigorous quantitative analysis using appropriate statistical methods (Cohen's D) and detailed examination of mark distributions. The 5% interval analysis (C52, C56) effectively rules out hidden gaps. Figure 3 provides clear visual evidence supporting the superimposed coursework distributions (C55) versus shifted exam distributions (C53).

results.result: Analysis of first-class marks confirmed the pattern: coursework gaps remained small (year 2: 2.60%, year 3: 4.11%) while exam gaps were 2+ times larger. In 3/4 year 3 courses, exam gaps exceeded coursework gaps for first-class marks. Overall, exams are the main contributor to the award gap, with coursework contribution being small and possibly inconsistent in years 1-2.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C61 extend the analysis to first-class marks specifically, confirming the exam-coursework pattern holds at this higher threshold. The quantitative data are clearly reported with appropriate comparisons. C60-C61 provide reasonable summary conclusions based on the comprehensive analysis, though they involve some inference about relative contributions.

results.result: The finding that exams produce larger gaps than coursework is consistent with medicine, where different assessment types produce gaps of different sizes, though exams versus coursework were not explicitly tested in that field.
results.evaluation: Claim C62 appropriately contextualizes the findings within existing literature while noting the limitation that the prior medical study did not explicitly test the exam-coursework distinction. The citation provides support for variable gaps by assessment type in another discipline.

results.result: Despite extensive reviews and hundreds of recommendations over the past decade, the award gap has only decreased by 0.5% per year. Analysis suggests this slow progress is due to lack of staff time and funding, limited scientific approaches and diverse evidence on causes, and insufficient funding for fundamental and applied research.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C67 are supported by citations documenting the slow rate of progress (C63) and extensive prior recommendations (C64). However, C65-C67 represent the author's inference from literature review rather than empirical findings. While the reasoning is plausible, these are interpretive claims about barriers to progress rather than directly measured outcomes.

results.result: Universities have identified ~200 recommendations across three reports, but these are time-intensive and costly to implement. Academics already work excessive hours, UK staff-student ratios are poor (not in top 100 globally), and current funding is only £8 per BAME student. The scale of the problem (>440,000 courses nationally) vastly exceeds current resources (handful of staff positions).
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C75 combine documented facts (C68: 200 recommendations; C70-C71: citations on workload and ratios; C73-C75: calculations from institutional data) with reasonable inferences about resource constraints (C69). The quantitative estimates (C73-C75) are clearly sourced from UCL records and government data, though the scaling calculation (C74) involves extrapolation.

results.result: Only 0.51% of recommendations appear supported by raw numerical data, while 20.3% are based on qualitative data (surveys, interviews). Many surveys (25/30) lack control data. A comprehensive analysis of 99 UK institutions identified 'a far more scientific approach' as one of the top five actions needed.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C79 present the author's systematic analysis of the evidence base for existing recommendations. While the percentages (C76-C77) are estimates from the author's review, the methodology is described in Methods and the conclusion is supported by citation to an independent comprehensive analysis (C78). The lack of control data (C79) is a valid methodological critique.

results.result: UK government funding for closing the award gap is only £3 million/year (£8 per BAME undergraduate), committed for only 2-3 years, yet the gap will take several decades to close at current projection (0.5% per year).
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C82 present calculations based on government funding data and student numbers (detailed in Methods). The per-student calculation (C80) is straightforward arithmetic. The projection (C82) is based on cited data about the current rate of closure (C63), making it a reasonable extrapolation though it assumes linear progress.

results.result: Closing the award gap would benefit all employers by reducing ethnicity pay and career gaps, increasing productivity through workforce diversity. It is the sole method for universities to address breach of UK race equality laws. The Dementia Discovery Fund (£250 million, £294 per patient) provides a model for stakeholder alliance funding.
results.evaluation: Claim C83 is speculative about broader economic benefits without supporting evidence. C84 makes a legal claim about UK equality law that may be oversimplified. C85 provides a factual comparison to another funding model, but the analogy's applicability to the award gap problem is not established. These claims support policy recommendations but lack empirical validation.

results.result: Pioneering PhD programs in UK and US (LIDo, Tetrad, APS Bridge) have achieved 2-4 fold increases in minority ethnic PhD students over 3-6 years, with higher retention than national averages. These programs share common features including holistic admissions and cohort support. New funding has been awarded to extend these approaches.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C90 are supported by citations and personal communications documenting successful programs. The specific programs are identified (C88) and their success metrics are cited (C86-C87). Claims about new funding (C89-C90) are based on knowledge of recent announcements. C91 adds context about student perspectives from a cited study.

results.result: Other inequalities contribute to outcomes: fewer students from deprived neighborhoods progress to higher education, and certain ethnic groups (Pakistani, Black, Roma/Gypsy/Irish/traveller) receive fewer high grades in end-of-school exams. Different solutions may be needed for different subjects given the 3-22% variation in award gaps.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C18 are supported by citations to studies documenting these additional inequalities. C22 is a reasonable inference from the documented subject variation (C21). These claims appropriately acknowledge the complexity of factors contributing to educational disparities beyond the specific focus of this study.

results.result: Terminology and demographics vary internationally. In the UK, BAME represents Black, Asian, mixed and other minority ethnic groups (14% of population). In the US, URM (underrepresented minority) is used, with 36% minority ethnic population. Asian Americans are overrepresented in PhD positions, linked to higher GRE scores.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C95 provide methodological context about terminology and international differences. These are based on established knowledge of demographic data and terminology conventions (C92-C94) and cited studies (C95). This contextual information is important for interpreting the study's findings and their generalizability.

results.result: Methodological details: UCL classifies completion as non-zero marks; 4.5% of students had missing component marks; most prior recommendations were based on informal observation (74.62%) or qualitative data (20.3%); 25/30 surveys lacked control data or didn't report respondent ethnicity; funding calculations are based on government data and student numbers; study predates COVID-19.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C108 provide essential methodological information and data sources. These include institutional definitions (C96), data completeness (C97), systematic analysis of prior evidence (C98-C101), funding calculations (C102-C107), and temporal context (C108). These are appropriately detailed in the Methods section and support the transparency and reproducibility of the study.
